source.text: בַּשָּׁנָ֣ה הַ֠תְּשִׁעִית לְצִדְקִיָּ֨הוּ מֶלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֜ה בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הָעֲשִׂרִ֗י בָּ֠א נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֨ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֤ל וְכָל־חֵילוֹ֙ אֶל־יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וַיָּצֻ֖רוּ עָלֶֽיהָ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: In the year the ninth of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the month the tenth, came Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and all his army to Jerusalem, and they besieged it.

en.L: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon came, and all his army, against Jerusalem, and they besieged it.
en.B: In the tenth month of the ninth year of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon advanced on Jerusalem with his whole army, and they laid siege to it.
en.R: In the ninth year that Zedekiah was king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadrezzar, the king of Babylon, marched against Jerusalem with his whole army. They surrounded the city and cut it off.

decisions.choice: the fall of Jerusalem told again: 2 Kings 25:1-12 and Jeremiah 52:4-16
decisions.reason: Verses 1-10 tell more briefly what 2 Kings 25:1-12 tells, and Jeremiah 52:4-16 repeats the Kings account almost word for word. This verse matches 2 Kings 25:1 except that it names Zedekiah instead of saying "his reign", gives the month but not the day, spells the king's name Nebuchadrezzar, and has one verb, "they besieged it", where Kings says that he camped against the city and they built siege works all around it. Where the Hebrew is the same, the wording here is the wording of 2 Kings 25.

decisions.choice: the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year: early in 588 BC
decisions.reason: As at 2 Kings 25:1: the tenth month falls in midwinter, early in 588 BC or a year earlier, depending on how the reign years were counted. Ezekiel 24:1-2 records the same day, and Zechariah 8:19 names "the fast of the tenth month" kept for it.

decisions.choice: verses 1-2 a brief summary set inside the story
decisions.reason: Chapter 38 ends with Jeremiah in the court of the guard "until the day Jerusalem was captured" and a clause that begins "when Jerusalem was captured". Verses 1-2 then give the dates of the siege and the breach, and verse 3 goes on with what happened when the city fell. The two verses read as a summary set into the story; they are kept here as sentences of their own.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar: the same king as Nebuchadnezzar
decisions.reason: Jeremiah usually spells the name with an r, Nebuchadrezzar, closer to the Babylonian Nabu-kudurri-usur; 2 Kings 25 spells it Nebuchadnezzar. Each verse keeps the form its own text uses (see 21:2).

decisions.choice: laid siege to it (Balanced); surrounded the city and cut it off (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a siege is instead of using the word, as at 2 Kings 25:2. Literal's "they besieged it" keeps the single Hebrew verb.

source.text: בְּעַשְׁתֵּֽי־עֶשְׂרֵ֤ה שָׁנָה֙ לְצִדְקִיָּ֔הוּ בַּחֹ֥דֶשׁ הָרְבִיעִ֖י בְּתִשְׁעָ֣ה לַחֹ֑דֶשׁ הָבְקְעָ֖ה הָעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: In [the] eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the month the fourth, on [the] ninth of the month, was broken into the city.

en.L: In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth [day] of the month, the city was broken into.
en.B: In the fourth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year, on the ninth day of the month, the city wall was breached.
en.R: Then on the ninth day of the fourth month, in Zedekiah's eleventh year as king, the enemy broke through the city wall.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:2-4 and Jeremiah 52:5-7 in one sentence
decisions.reason: Kings tells this in three steps: the city was under siege until Zedekiah's eleventh year, on the ninth of the month the famine was severe, and the city was broken into (2 Kings 25:2-4). This verse gives only the year, the full date and the breach, and leaves out the famine. It also names the fourth month, which the Hebrew of 2 Kings 25:3 lacks.

decisions.choice: the ninth day of the fourth month: midsummer, about a year and a half after the siege began
decisions.reason: From the tenth month of the ninth year (verse 1) to the fourth month of the eleventh is about eighteen months. The day fell in midsummer of 586 BC or a year earlier, and "the fast of the fourth month" was later kept for it (Zechariah 8:19).

decisions.choice: was broken into: a breach was made in the city wall
decisions.reason: The verb means to split open. It is used of a city whose wall is breached so that the enemy can enter (2 Kings 25:4; Ezekiel 26:10).

decisions.choice: [day] (Literal); the city wall (Balanced, Readable); the enemy (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:3-4: Literal brackets "day", Balanced and Readable say it was the wall that was breached, and Readable names who broke through.

source.text: וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ כֹּ֚ל שָׂרֵ֣י מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֔ל וַיֵּשְׁב֖וּ בְּשַׁ֣עַר הַתָּ֑וֶךְ נֵרְגַ֣ל שַׂר־אֶ֠צֶר סַֽמְגַּר־נְב֞וּ שַׂר־סְכִ֣ים רַב־סָרִ֗יס נֵרְגַ֤ל שַׂר־אֶ֨צֶר֙ רַב־מָ֔ג וְכָל־שְׁאֵרִ֔ית שָׂרֵ֖י מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And came all [the] princes of [the] king of Babylon and sat in [the] gate of the middle: Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebu, Sarsekim [the] Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer [the] Rab-mag, and all [the] rest of [the] princes of [the] king of Babylon.

en.L: And all the princes of the king of Babylon came and sat in the Middle Gate: Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebu, Sarsekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag, and all the rest of the princes of the king of Babylon.
en.B: Then all the officials of the king of Babylon came in and took their seats in the Middle Gate: Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebu, Sarsekim the chief of the court officials, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag, and all the other officials of the king of Babylon.
en.R: Then all the leaders who served the king of Babylon came and sat down in the Middle Gate. They were Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebu, Sarsekim the head of the palace officials, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag, who was a high officer, and all the other leaders of the king of Babylon.

decisions.choice: sat in the Middle Gate: took control of the city
decisions.reason: The gate was where those in authority sat to judge and to govern (Ruth 4:1-2; 38:7). By sitting there the Babylonian officers showed that the city was now theirs. The LORD had said at Jeremiah's call that the kings of the north would come and each set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem (1:15).

decisions.choice: the Middle Gate: a gate inside the city, its place unknown
decisions.reason: This gate is named only here. It may have stood in a wall between two parts of the city, such as the older city and the newer quarter to its north.

decisions.choice: four men named as the Hebrew divides the words: Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebu, Sarsekim, Nergal-sharezer
alternatives: Nergal-sharezer of Sin-magir, Nebu-sarsekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag
decisions.reason: The names are Babylonian, and how the words divide into names and titles is disputed. Nergal-sharezer (Nergal-shar-usur, "may Nergal protect the king") appears twice, the second time as the Rab-mag; he may be one man named twice, and he is often taken to be the Neriglissar who later became king of Babylon (560-556 BC). "Samgar" may be the Babylonian district Sin-magir, a title of the first Nergal-sharezer, and "nebu" may belong to the following name, giving Nebu-sarsekim the Rab-saris. A Babylonian tablet from Nebuchadrezzar's reign names a chief court official Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, which may be the same name. Read that way, the verse names two or three men, not four. The text is kept as the Hebrew divides it.

decisions.choice: Rab-saris and Rab-mag: titles of high Babylonian officers
decisions.reason: Rab-saris is the chief of the court officials, the title of an Assyrian officer in 2 Kings 18:17; its second part is the word used for eunuchs or court officials. Rab-mag is a Babylonian title for a high officer of the court; its exact office is not known. Both are titles, not names.

decisions.choice: princes (Literal); officials (Balanced); leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: The wording settled for the Hebrew word for a king's high officers.

decisions.choice: the chief of the court officials, the head of the palace officials; Rab-mag kept
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable translate Rab-saris as 2 Kings 18:17 does. Rab-mag is kept as a title at every level because its meaning is not known; Readable adds that it was a high office.

source.text: וַיְהִ֡י כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר רָ֠אָם צִדְקִיָּ֨הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֜ה וְכֹ֣ל׀אַנְשֵׁ֣י הַמִּלְחָמָ֗ה וַֽ֠יִּבְרְחוּ וַיֵּצְא֨וּ לַ֤יְלָה מִן־הָעִיר֙ דֶּ֚רֶךְ גַּ֣ן הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ בְּשַׁ֖עַר בֵּ֣ין הַחֹמֹתָ֑יִם וַיֵּצֵ֖א דֶּ֥רֶךְ הָעֲרָבָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, when saw them Zedekiah king of Judah and all [the] men of the war, and they fled and went out by night from the city [by the] way of [the] garden of the king, by [the] gate between the two walls; and he went out [the] way of the Arabah.

en.L: And it came about, when Zedekiah king of Judah and all the men of war saw them, [that] they fled and went out of the city by night by way of the king's garden, through the gate between the two walls; and he went out by way of the Arabah.
en.B: When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers caught sight of them, they fled. They went out of the city at night, taking the road by the king's garden, through the gate between the two walls, and the king went off toward the Arabah.
en.R: Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them and ran away. That night they slipped out of the city along the path by the king's garden, through the gate between the two walls. King Zedekiah fled toward the Jordan Valley.

decisions.choice: verses 4-13 are part of the Hebrew text but are not in the Greek
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation of Jeremiah, which is shorter than the Hebrew throughout (see 1:1), does not have verses 4-13: it goes from the officers in the gate (verse 3) to their sending for Jeremiah (verse 14). These verses tell much that is also in 2 Kings 25:4-12 and Jeremiah 52:7-16.

decisions.choice: saw them: the Babylonian officers sitting in the gate
decisions.reason: The nearest people named are the officials of verse 3. When the king and his soldiers saw that the enemy were already inside and holding the gate, they knew the city was lost.

decisions.choice: the king's garden and the gate between the two walls: at the south end of the city
decisions.reason: As at 2 Kings 25:4: the king's garden lay at the south end of Jerusalem near the Pool of Siloam (Nehemiah 3:15), and a gate there between two lines of wall led down into the valley.

decisions.choice: he went out: Zedekiah, toward the Arabah, the Jordan Valley
decisions.reason: The verb is singular: the king led the flight. The Arabah is the deep valley of the Jordan running down to the Dead Sea; Zedekiah was making for the river crossings near Jericho.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:4 told with more detail
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:4 says only that the city was broken into and the soldiers left by night, with no verb for their going and without naming the king. This verse adds that Zedekiah and the soldiers saw the officers, "fled and went out" (as Jeremiah 52:7), names the king, puts the garden before the gate, and does not say that the Chaldeans were all around the city.

decisions.choice: soldiers (Balanced, Readable); the king, King Zedekiah; the Jordan Valley (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:4: "the men of war" are the soldiers, Balanced says "the king" for "he", and Readable names him and explains the Arabah.

source.text: וַיִּרְדְּפ֨וּ חֵיל־כַּשְׂדִּ֜ים אַחֲרֵיהֶ֗ם וַיַּשִּׂ֣גוּ אֶת־צִדְקִיָּהוּ֮ בְּעַֽרְב֣וֹת יְרֵחוֹ֒ וַיִּקְח֣וּ אֹת֗וֹ וַֽ֠יַּעֲלֻהוּ אֶל־נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֧ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֛ל רִבְלָ֖תָה בְּאֶ֣רֶץ חֲמָ֑ת וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ מִשְׁפָּטִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And pursued [the] army of [the] Chaldeans after them, and overtook Zedekiah in [the] plains of Jericho; and they took him and brought him up to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon [to] Riblah in [the] land of Hamath, and he spoke with him judgments.

en.L: And the army of the Chaldeans pursued them, and they overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho; and they took him and brought him up to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he spoke judgments with him.
en.B: But the Chaldean army chased them and caught up with Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. They seized him and took him up to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and there the king passed sentence on him.
en.R: But the Babylonian army chased after them and caught up with Zedekiah on the plains near Jericho. They captured him and took him to Nebuchadrezzar, the king of Babylon, at the town of Riblah in the land of Hamath. There Nebuchadrezzar put him on trial and sentenced him.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:5-6 with small differences
decisions.reason: Kings has the army pursue "the king" and adds that his army scattered from him; this verse has "them", names Zedekiah, and leaves out the scattering. It names Nebuchadrezzar, adds that Riblah is "in the land of Hamath" (as Jeremiah 52:9), and has "he spoke judgments", one judge and a plural noun, where Kings has "they spoke judgment".

decisions.choice: the plains of Jericho and Riblah in the land of Hamath
decisions.reason: Jericho lies in the Jordan Valley some fifteen miles east of Jerusalem and far below it. Riblah stood on the Orontes River in Syria, far to the north, where Nebuchadrezzar directed his campaign (as at 2 Kings 25:5-6).

decisions.choice: spoke judgments with him: tried him and passed sentence
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of bringing a legal case against someone (1:16; 4:12; 52:9). Zedekiah was judged as a vassal who had broken his oath of loyalty (2 Kings 24:20; Ezekiel 17:13-20). The plural may mean the charges and the sentence together.

decisions.choice: Zedekiah before the king of Babylon, as Jeremiah had said
decisions.reason: Jeremiah had told Zedekiah that he would be handed over to the king of Babylon and see him face to face (32:4; 34:3).

decisions.choice: the king, Nebuchadrezzar (Balanced, Readable); Babylonian (Readable); put him on trial and sentenced him (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:5-6. Balanced and Readable name the one Hebrew calls "he", and Readable spells out the legal sense of the idiom.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁחַט֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ בָּבֶ֜ל אֶת־בְּנֵ֧י צִדְקִיָּ֛הוּ בְּרִבְלָ֖ה לְעֵינָ֑יו וְאֵת֙ כָּל־חֹרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה שָׁחַ֖ט מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And slaughtered [the] king of Babylon [the] sons of Zedekiah in Riblah before his eyes; and all [the] nobles of Judah slaughtered [the] king of Babylon.

en.L: And the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes; and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah.
en.B: At Riblah the king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah's sons while he watched; the king of Babylon also slaughtered all the nobles of Judah.
en.R: At Riblah the king of Babylon killed Zedekiah's sons while Zedekiah watched. He also killed all the leading men of Judah.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:7 names no killer and no nobles
decisions.reason: Kings says "they slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes". This verse names the king of Babylon as the one who did it, adds "at Riblah", and adds that he also killed all the nobles of Judah. Jeremiah 52:10 has the same addition with the word for officials instead of nobles.

decisions.choice: nobles: the freeborn leading men of Judah
decisions.reason: The word names men of high birth and standing, set beside the officials in Nehemiah 2:16 and used of the leading men taken with Jehoiachin (27:20). These were the men who had led the rebellion with the king.

decisions.choice: the sons killed before his eyes
decisions.reason: As at 2 Kings 25:7: killing a rebel king's sons ended his line, and it was the last thing Zedekiah saw.

decisions.choice: while Zedekiah watched; He; the leading men (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable names Zedekiah so that "he" is not taken for the king of Babylon, uses "he" for the repeated "the king of Babylon", and says "leading men" for "nobles".

source.text: וְאֶת־עֵינֵ֥י צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ עִוֵּ֑ר וַיַּאַסְרֵ֨הוּ֙ בַּֽנְחֻשְׁתַּ֔יִם לָבִ֥יא אֹת֖וֹ בָּבֶֽלָה׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] eyes of Zedekiah he blinded, and bound him in bronze fetters to bring him [to] Babylon.

en.L: And he put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in bronze fetters to bring him [to] Babylon.
en.B: Then he put out Zedekiah's eyes and bound him in bronze fetters to take him to Babylon.
en.R: Then he had Zedekiah's eyes put out. He had him bound in bronze chains to be taken to Babylon.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:7: "and brought him to Babylon"
decisions.reason: Kings ends "and brought him to Babylon"; this verse says he bound him "to bring him" there, the purpose rather than the journey. Jeremiah 52:11 adds that Zedekiah was kept in prison until his death. The one who blinds him is the king of Babylon of verse 6.

decisions.choice: the prophets' words come true
decisions.reason: Jeremiah had told Zedekiah that he would see the king of Babylon and be taken to Babylon (32:4-5; 34:3), and Ezekiel had said that the prince would be brought to Babylon "but he will not see it" (Ezekiel 12:13). Both came true.

decisions.choice: bronze fetters: a pair of bronze shackles
decisions.reason: As at 2 Kings 25:7: the word is "bronze" in the dual form, a pair of shackles (Judges 16:21).

decisions.choice: had ... put out; had him bound; chains (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:7: Readable says the king "had" these things done, and says "chains" for fetters.

source.text: וְאֶת־בֵּ֤ית הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְאֶת־בֵּ֣ית הָעָ֔ם שָׂרְפ֥וּ הַכַּשְׂדִּ֖ים בָּאֵ֑שׁ וְאֶת־חֹמ֥וֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם נָתָֽצוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] house of the king and [the] house of the people burned the Chaldeans with fire, and [the] walls of Jerusalem they broke down.

en.L: And the Chaldeans burned the house of the king and the house of the people with fire, and they broke down the walls of Jerusalem.
en.B: The Chaldeans burned down the king's palace and the houses of the people, and they tore down the walls of Jerusalem.
en.R: The Babylonians set fire to the royal palace and the people's houses, and they tore down the walls of Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the house of the people: the houses of the city's people
decisions.reason: The noun is singular, but it may stand for all the people's houses, as 2 Kings 25:9 says "all the houses of Jerusalem". It may instead name one public building, a hall where the people met.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:9-10 also names the temple
decisions.reason: Kings dates the burning to a month after the city fell, makes Nebuzaradan the one who burned it, and names the house of the LORD first. This verse names only the king's house and the house of the people, and says the Chaldeans did it; the burning of the temple is told in 52:13.

decisions.choice: the walls broken down: the city left without defense
decisions.reason: As at 2 Kings 25:10: without walls a city could not protect itself. They lay in ruins until Nehemiah rebuilt them (Nehemiah 1:3; 2:17).

decisions.choice: the king's palace, the royal palace; the houses of the people; Babylonians (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:9. Balanced and Readable take the singular "house of the people" as the people's houses (m1).

source.text: וְאֵת֩ יֶ֨תֶר הָעָ֜ם הַנִּשְׁאָרִ֣ים בָּעִ֗יר וְאֶת־הַנֹּֽפְלִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָפְל֣וּ עָלָ֔יו וְאֵ֛ת יֶ֥תֶר הָעָ֖ם הַנִּשְׁאָרִ֑ים הֶגְלָ֛ה נְבֽוּזַר־אֲדָ֥ןרַב־טַבָּחִ֖ים בָּבֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] rest of the people who remained in the city, and the deserters who had fallen to him, and [the] rest of the people who remained, exiled Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards [to] Babylon.

en.L: And the rest of the people who were left in the city, and the deserters who had deserted to him, and the rest of the people who were left, Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard carried into exile [to] Babylon.
en.B: Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the rest of the people who remained.
en.R: Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took the rest of the people away to Babylon as captives. These included the people still left in the city, those who had gone over to his side, and everyone else who remained.

decisions.choice: fell to him: deserted to him
decisions.reason: To "fall to" an enemy is to go over to his side (21:9; 37:13-14; 38:19). "Him" is the king of Babylon, as 2 Kings 25:11 says, or his commander Nebuzaradan.

decisions.choice: Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard: a senior Babylonian officer
decisions.reason: As at 2 Kings 25:8: the title is literally "chief of the slaughterers", the king's bodyguard. Nebuzaradan is the Babylonian name Nabu-zer-iddin.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:11 with small differences
decisions.reason: Kings has "deserted to the king of Babylon" where this verse has "to him", and ends the list with "the rest of the multitude", where this verse repeats "the rest of the people who remained" (Jeremiah 52:15 has a word for craftsmen). This verse adds "to Babylon". The date of Nebuzaradan's coming, given in 2 Kings 25:8, is not here.

decisions.choice: Nebuzaradan ... carried into exile (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:11: Literal keeps the Hebrew order, with the groups first and the verb and subject last; Balanced and Readable begin with Nebuzaradan.

source.text: וּמִן־הָעָ֣ם הַדַּלִּ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר אֵין־לָהֶם֙ מְא֔וּמָה הִשְׁאִ֛יר נְבוּזַרְאֲדָ֥ן רַב־טַבָּחִ֖ים בְּאֶ֣רֶץ יְהוּדָ֑ה וַיִּתֵּ֥ן לָהֶ֛ם כְּרָמִ֥ים וִֽיגֵבִ֖ים בַּיּ֥וֹם הַהֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: And some of the people the poor who [there was] nothing to them, left Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards in [the] land of Judah; and he gave to them vineyards and fields on the day the that.

en.L: But some of the poor people, who had nothing, Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard left in the land of Judah; and he gave them vineyards and fields on that day.
en.B: But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and at that time he gave them vineyards and fields.
en.R: But Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, left behind in the land of Judah some of the poorest people, who owned nothing. At that time he gave them vineyards and fields.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:12: left as vinedressers and field workers
decisions.reason: Kings says the captain left some of the poorest of the land as vinedressers and field workers. This verse says they owned nothing, that they were left "in the land of Judah", and that he gave them vineyards and fields.

decisions.choice: fields: farmland, a word found only here
decisions.reason: The word appears nowhere else, and its sense comes from its place beside "vineyards" and from the related word for field workers in 2 Kings 25:12. It names land for crops.

decisions.choice: the landless given land
decisions.reason: The people who had owned nothing were left in the land and given the vineyards and fields of those taken away. The exile of the powerful turned the poor into landholders.

decisions.choice: on that day: at that time
decisions.reason: The phrase ties the gift to the time of the exile, not to one particular day.

decisions.choice: at that time (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom (m4); Literal keeps "on that day".

source.text: וַיְצַ֛ו נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֥ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֖ל עַֽל־יִרְמְיָ֑הוּ בְּיַ֛ד נְבוּזַרְאֲדָ֥ן רַב־טַבָּחִ֖ים לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And commanded Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon concerning Jeremiah by [the] hand of Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards, saying,

en.L: And Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah by the hand of Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard, saying,
en.B: Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon had given orders about Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, saying,
en.R: Nebuchadrezzar, the king of Babylon, had given Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, orders about Jeremiah. He said,

decisions.choice: by the hand of Nebuzaradan: through him, for him to carry out
decisions.reason: "By the hand of" someone means through him as the agent. The king sent the order by Nebuzaradan, who was to see it done.

decisions.choice: commanded: an order given before the officers acted
decisions.reason: The verb simply continues the story, but the king was at Riblah (verse 5), far from Jerusalem, so the order must have been sent earlier, before the officers took Jeremiah out (verses 13-14).

decisions.choice: why the king cared about Jeremiah
decisions.reason: The text gives no reason. The Babylonians may have heard that Jeremiah had urged the city to surrender (21:9; 38:2, 17); those who deserted would have reported it. Chapter 40:2-3 puts in Nebuzaradan's mouth the view that the LORD had brought this disaster on the city because of its sin, as Jeremiah had said.

decisions.choice: not in the Greek
decisions.reason: This verse is part of the section absent from the Greek translation (see verse 4).

decisions.choice: had given orders (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the past perfect to show that the order came before the events of verses 13-14 (m2). Readable makes the order a sentence of its own.

source.text: קָחֶ֗נּוּ וְעֵינֶ֨יךָ֙ שִׂ֣ים עָלָ֔יו וְאַל־תַּ֥עַשׂ ל֖וֹ מְא֣וּמָה רָּ֑ע כִּ֗י כַּֽאֲשֶׁר֙ יְדַבֵּ֣ר אֵלֶ֔יךָ כֵּ֖ן עֲשֵׂ֥ה עִמּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Take him, and your eyes set on him, and do not do to him anything harmful; but just as he will speak to you, so do with him.

en.L: "Take him and set your eyes on him, and do not do anything harmful to him; but just as he speaks to you, so do with him."
en.B: "Take him and look after him. Do him no harm, but do for him whatever he asks of you."
en.R: "Take Jeremiah and look after him. Do not hurt him in any way. Do for him whatever he asks you to do."

decisions.choice: set your eyes on him: watch over him with care
decisions.reason: To set one's eyes on someone is to keep watch over him for his good (40:4; Genesis 44:21). The order is for Jeremiah's protection.

decisions.choice: as he speaks to you, so do with him: let Jeremiah's own wishes decide
decisions.reason: Jeremiah himself is to say what is done with him. In 40:4-5 Nebuzaradan offers him the choice of going to Babylon or staying in the land.

decisions.choice: not in the Greek
decisions.reason: As in verse 4.

decisions.choice: Jeremiah (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable names the man the order is about.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֞ח נְבֽוּזַרְאֲדָ֣ן רַב־טַבָּחִ֗ים וּנְבֽוּשַׁזְבָּן֙רַב־סָרִ֔יס וְנֵרְגַ֥ל שַׂר־אֶ֖צֶר רַב־מָ֑ג וְכֹ֖ל רַבֵּ֥י מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards, and Nebushazban [the] Rab-saris, and Nergal-sharezer [the] Rab-mag, and all [the] chiefs of [the] king of Babylon,

en.L: And Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard sent, and Nebushazban the Rab-saris, and Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon,
en.B: So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the chief of the court officials, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag and all the king of Babylon's chief officers sent word,
en.R: So Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, sent for Jeremiah. With him were Nebushazban, the head of the palace officials, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag, and all the other chief officers of the king of Babylon.

decisions.choice: Nebushazban the Rab-saris: a chief court official not named in verse 3
decisions.reason: Verse 3 names Sarsekim as the Rab-saris; here the title goes with Nebushazban (Nabu-shezibanni, "Nabu, save me"). Two men may have held the title at different times, or the names in verse 3 are to be divided differently (see verse 3). Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag is the man named last in verse 3.

decisions.choice: sent: the sentence continues in verse 14
decisions.reason: The verb is singular, agreeing with Nebuzaradan, who is named first and acts for the rest. What they sent to do follows in verse 14, which repeats "they sent".

decisions.choice: the chief officers: the great men of the king's court
decisions.reason: The word is the plural of "chief", the first part of the titles Rab-saris and Rab-mag. It is a different word from the "princes" of verse 3, but it names the same group of high officers.

decisions.choice: not in the Greek
decisions.reason: This verse ends the section absent from the Greek translation (see verse 4).

decisions.choice: sent word (Balanced); sent for Jeremiah (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the verb an object; Readable names Jeremiah and makes the list of officers a second sentence.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלְחוּ֩ וַיִּקְח֨וּ אֶֽת־יִרְמְיָ֜הוּ מֵחֲצַ֣ר הַמַּטָּרָ֗ה וַיִּתְּנ֤וּ אֹתוֹ֙ אֶל־גְּדַלְיָ֨הוּ֙ בֶּן־אֲחִיקָ֣ם בֶּן־שָׁפָ֔ן לְהוֹצִאֵ֖הוּ אֶל־הַבָּ֑יִת וַיֵּ֖שֶׁב בְּת֥וֹךְ הָעָֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: and they sent and took Jeremiah from [the] court of the guard, and gave him to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan to bring him out to the house; and he stayed among the people.

en.L: and they sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard, and they gave him to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, to bring him out to the house; and he stayed among the people.
en.B: and had Jeremiah brought from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, to take him home, and he stayed among the people.
en.R: They had Jeremiah brought out of the courtyard of the guard and put him in the care of Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, who was to take him home. So Jeremiah stayed among the people who were left in the land.

decisions.choice: the court of the guard: a courtyard of the palace where prisoners were held
decisions.reason: Jeremiah had been kept there under guard (32:2; 37:21) and had stayed there after he was lifted out of the cistern, until the day Jerusalem was captured (38:13, 28).

decisions.choice: Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan
decisions.reason: Gedaliah came from a family of royal officials who had stood by Jeremiah: his father Ahikam had protected him (26:24), and his grandfather Shaphan was King Josiah's secretary (2 Kings 22:3). The king of Babylon made Gedaliah governor of those left in Judah (40:5; 2 Kings 25:22).

decisions.choice: to bring him out to the house: to take him home
decisions.reason: "The house" is not named. It may be Gedaliah's house or simply home, away from the prison; either way Jeremiah was set free into Gedaliah's care.

decisions.choice: 40:1-6 tells of Jeremiah's release at Ramah
decisions.reason: Chapter 40 says that Nebuzaradan found Jeremiah bound in chains among the captives at Ramah, freed him there and sent him to Gedaliah. The text does not say how the two accounts fit: Jeremiah may have been freed here, then caught up among the captives, and freed again, or the two passages may tell the same release in different ways.

decisions.choice: the Greek resumes here
decisions.reason: The Greek translation goes on from verse 3 to this verse (see verse 4).

decisions.choice: the people who were left in the land (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says who "the people" were: those not taken into exile (verse 10).

decisions.choice: had Jeremiah brought (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "Sent and took" means they sent men to fetch him; Balanced and Readable say so with "had ... brought". Balanced has already said "sent word" at the end of verse 13, so it does not repeat "they sent".

source.text: וְאֶֽל־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ הָיָ֣ה דְבַר־יְהוָ֑ה בִּֽהְיֹת֣וֹ עָצ֔וּר בַּחֲצַ֥ר הַמַּטָּרָ֖ה לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And to Jeremiah came [the] word of Yahweh while he was shut up in [the] court of the guard, saying,

en.L: And the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had come to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard, saying:
en.B: The word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had come to Jeremiah while he was confined in the court of the guard:
en.R: While Jeremiah was still locked up in the courtyard of the guard, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had given him this message:

decisions.choice: had come: a word given earlier, while Jeremiah was still a prisoner
decisions.reason: Putting "to Jeremiah" first marks a step back in time. The word came after Ebed-melech had rescued him from the cistern (38:7-13), while he was still held in the court of the guard (38:28), before the city fell.

decisions.choice: shut up: kept confined, under guard
decisions.reason: The same word is used of Jeremiah in 33:1 and 36:5. He could not leave the court of the guard.

decisions.choice: had come; had given (past perfect at every level)
decisions.reason: The past perfect shows that this word came before the events just told (m1). The rest follows the settled wording of "the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD".

source.text: הָל֣וֹךְ וְאָמַרְתָּ֡ לְעֶבֶד־מֶ֨לֶךְהַכּוּשִׁ֜י לֵאמֹ֗ר כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל הִנְנִי֩ מֵבִ֨יא אֶת־דְּבָרַ֜י אֶל־הָעִ֥יר הַזֹּ֛את לְרָעָ֖ה וְלֹ֣א לְטוֹבָ֑ה וְהָי֥וּ לְפָנֶ֖יךָ בַּיּ֥וֹם הַהֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: Go, and you will say to Ebed-melech the Cushite, saying, Thus says Yahweh of hosts, God of Israel: Here I [am] bringing my words to the city the this for harm and not for good, and they will be before you on the day the that.

en.L: "Go and say to Ebed-melech the Cushite: 'Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, the God of Israel: Look, I am bringing {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words against this city for disaster and not for good, and they will happen before you on that day.
en.B: "Go and tell Ebed-melech the Cushite, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says this: Look, I am about to carry out {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words against this city, for disaster and not for good. On that day you will see them come true.
en.R: "Go and tell Ebed-melech, the man from Cush, 'This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says: I am going to do to this city what I said I would do. I will bring disaster on it, not good. On that day you will see it happen.

decisions.choice: Ebed-melech the Cushite: the court official who rescued Jeremiah
decisions.reason: His name means "servant of the king". He came from Cush, the land on the Nile south of Egypt, and served in Zedekiah's palace. He had pleaded with the king for Jeremiah and pulled him up out of the cistern (38:7-13).

decisions.choice: bring my words against this city for disaster and not for good: carry out what I have said
decisions.reason: To "bring" one's words is to make them happen. "For disaster and not for good" is said of the LORD's purpose for the city in 21:10 and 44:27.

decisions.choice: they will be before you: you will see them happen
decisions.reason: "Before you" means in your sight. Ebed-melech would live to see the city fall.

decisions.choice: Thus says the LORD of hosts / of Armies; Look (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: The settled wording for these formulas in Jeremiah. Readable leaves out "Look", since "I am going to" already carries the sense that it is about to happen.

decisions.choice: the man from Cush (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says where he came from instead of using "Cushite".

source.text: וְהִצַּלְתִּ֥יךָ בַיּוֹם־הַה֖וּא נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה וְלֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ בְּיַ֣ד הָֽאֲנָשִׁ֔ים אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֥ה יָג֖וֹר מִפְּנֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: But I will deliver you on the day the that, declaration of Yahweh, and you will not be given into [the] hand of the men whom you [are] afraid of them.

en.L: But I will deliver you on that day, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and you will not be given into the hand of the men whom you fear.
en.B: But I will rescue you on that day, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; you will not be handed over to the men you are afraid of.
en.R: But I will save you on that day, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. You will not be handed over to the men you are afraid of.

decisions.choice: the men you fear: the Babylonians, or the leaders of Judah
decisions.reason: The text does not say who they are. They may be the Babylonians who would take the city, or the officials of Judah who had wanted Jeremiah dead (38:4) and whom Ebed-melech had opposed by rescuing him. Either way, the promise is that he will not fall into their power.

decisions.choice: deliver: rescue, snatch away from danger
decisions.reason: The verb is used of pulling someone out of the power of an enemy (1:8, 19; 15:20-21).

decisions.choice: says the LORD (Readable)
decisions.reason: The settled wording for this formula at Readable.

source.text: כִּ֤י מַלֵּט֙ אֲמַלֶּטְךָ֔ וּבַחֶ֖רֶב לֹ֣א תִפֹּ֑ל וְהָיְתָ֨ה לְךָ֤ נַפְשְׁךָ֙ לְשָׁלָ֔ל כִּֽי־בָטַ֥חְתָּ בִּ֖י נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: For surely I will rescue you, and by the sword you will not fall; and will be to you your life for plunder, because you trusted in me, declaration of Yahweh.

en.L: For I will surely rescue you, and you will not fall by the sword; and your life will be yours as plunder, because you have trusted in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"
en.B: I will certainly rescue you; you will not fall by the sword. You will come away with your life as your plunder, because you have trusted in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"
en.R: I will surely save you. You will not be killed in the war. You will escape with your life, because you trusted in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.'"

decisions.choice: your life will be yours as plunder: you will escape with your life
decisions.reason: The saying of 21:9 and 38:2, also given to Baruch (45:5). Plunder is what a soldier carries off from battle; Ebed-melech will carry off his own life from the ruin of the city. Here it is a promise of rescue, a reward for his trust.

decisions.choice: because you trusted in me
decisions.reason: The city trusted in lying words and in its temple (7:4, 8); the man who trusted in the LORD is the one who is saved (17:7-8). Ebed-melech's trust showed in what he did: he stood up for the LORD's prophet when others wanted him dead (38:7-13).

decisions.choice: surely rescue: the verb doubled for emphasis
decisions.reason: The Hebrew repeats the verb, "rescuing I will rescue you", to make the promise certain.

decisions.choice: come away with your life as your plunder (Balanced); escape with your life (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the wording of 21:9. Balanced follows 21:9 but leaves out "only", and Readable leaves out "and that will be all you get", because here the saying is a promise, not a warning. Readable says "killed in the war" for falling by the sword.
